title: 19  Clinical Sample-Size Calculation
text:
19.1 Main Functions
Sample size is determined by effect size, variability, confidence level, power, and study design; it is not a fixed constant. This chapter covers the three sample-size problems implemented by ivdtools: Bland–Altman agreement precision/power, precision of a single-proportion confidence interval, and a one-arm test of a proportion against a target.
All three functions are parameter-driven and do not require raw data. They return structured results; the sample size is in result$n, and print() shows target and achieved quantities. Round-up, attrition, invalid samples, and minimum stratum counts must be handled separately.

title: 19  Clinical Sample-Size Calculation
text:
Function
Main purpose
Solving direction




sample_size_bland_altman()
Bland–Altman agreement evaluation
Solve for n from target power


sample_size_proportion_ci()
Single-proportion confidence interval
Solve for n from the target half-width


sample_size_proportion()
One-arm target-value test
Solve for n from the target alpha and power





19.1.1 Interfaces


Code
sample_size_bland_altman(
  power = 0.80, mu, sd, delta,
  conf.level = 0.95, agree.level = 0.95,
  method = "lu", n.min = 3, n.max = 1e5
)
sample_size_proportion_ci(
  p, half_width, conf.level = 0.95,
  interval = c("two.sided", "lower", "upper"),
  method = "wilson", n.max = 1e6
)
sample_size_proportion(
  p0, p1, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80,
  alternative = c("greater", "less", "two.sided"),
  test = "exact", power_method = "binomial", n.max = 1e6
)


For Bland–Altman, the target LoA are
\[
\mu\pm z_{(1+\gamma)/2}\sigma,
\]
where $γ=agree.level. The function uses the Lu et al. noncentral-t calculation for the probability that both LoA confidence bounds remain within \(±\delta\) and searches for the smallest integer meeting target power. It requires \(δ>|\mu|+z_{(1+γ)/2}σ\).
For a proportion interval, the target is a half-width \(d\). For two-sided intervals,
\[\frac{U-L}{2}\le d,\]
and for one-sided intervals the distance from the expected proportion to the relevant limit is at most \(d\). The interval method affects the required sample size and must be stated in the protocol.
For a one-arm test, test determines the rejection region and power_method chooses continuous normal planning or discrete binomial enumeration. The final integer sample size is checked using actual alpha and achieved power; binomial planning additionally controls actual alpha rather than relying on an approximation.

title: 19  Clinical Sample-Size Calculation
text:
19.2 Analysis Examples

19.2.1 Bland–Altman Agreement


Code
n_ba <- sample_size_bland_altman(
  power = 0.80, mu = 0.2, sd = 1, delta = 2.5
)
print(n_ba)


Sample size for Bland-Altman agreement assessment
  Method            : Lu et al. (2016), noncentral-t approximation
  Mean difference   : 0.2000
  SD of differences : 1.0000
  Clinical limit    : 2.5000
  Confidence level  : 0.9500
  Agreement level   : 0.9500
  Sample size (n)   : 201
  Target power      : 0.800000
  Achieved power    : 0.800300


Under these teaching parameters, approximately 201 pairs are needed for 80% power. mu is mean difference, sd is difference SD, and delta is the clinical agreement limit. conf.level and agree.level describe different layers: reliability of the LoA estimate versus coverage of the LoA itself.


19.2.2 Single-Proportion Confidence Interval


Code
n_pci <- sample_size_proportion_ci(p = 0.3, half_width = 0.05)
print(n_pci)


Sample size for a single-proportion confidence interval
  Method                : wilson
  Interval              : two.sided
  Anticipated proportion: 0.3000
  Confidence level      : 0.9500
  Sample size (n)       : 320
  Target half-width     : 0.050000
  Achieved half-width   : 0.049967
  Target total width    : 0.100000
  Achieved total width  : 0.099934
  Planning interval     : [0.252406, 0.352339]
  Actual coverage       : 0.956096
  Actual alpha          : 0.043904


For expected proportion 0.3 and a 95% Wilson half-width of 0.05, approximately 320 observations are needed. Available methods include Wilson, Wald, continuity-corrected Wald/Wilson, Agresti–Coull, Jeffreys, and Clopper–Pearson.


19.2.3 One-Arm Target-Value Test


Code
n_sp <- sample_size_proportion(
  p0 = 0.2, p1 = 0.35, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8,
  alternative = "greater", test = "exact", power_method = "binomial"
)
print(n_sp)


Sample size for a single-proportion target-value test
  Test                  : Exact binomial test
  Power calculation     : Binomial enumeration
  H0: p <= 0.2000
  H1: p > 0.2000
  Expected p            : 0.3500
  Sample size (n)       : 56
  Target alpha          : 0.050000
  Actual alpha          : 0.043209
  Alpha criterion       : met
  Target power          : 0.800000
  Achieved power        : 0.806416 (binomial evaluation)
  Critical successes    : >= 17


alternative="greater" requires \(p_1>p_0\); use "less" or "two.sided" as appropriate. Exact, score, continuity-corrected score, Wald, and related test definitions are not interchangeable. Specify both test and power_method in the protocol.


19.2.4 Standard and Guidance Cross-Checks
The supplied examples compare the functions with PASS, SAS, and CMDE calculations. Small differences can arise from continuous normal planning versus discrete binomial enumeration, exact quantiles versus rounded handbook quantiles, interval definitions, and integer search rules. For example, a handbook may report a rounded approximate sample size while the package returns the first integer whose actual operating characteristics meet the stated constraint. Report both the selected method and achieved alpha/power.

title: 19  Clinical Sample-Size Calculation
text:
19.3 Interpretation Checklist

Define the primary endpoint, analysis unit, expected proportion or difference, allowable error, and tail direction.
Run sensitivity analyses for uncertain SDs, proportions, prevalence, and agreement limits.
Select interval and test methods before calculating the sample size.
Add attrition, invalid-sample, stratification, clustering, and multiple-endpoint allowances outside these functions.
Save parameters, function calls, outputs, and the software version in the protocol.

19.4 Complete Standard Cases

19.4.1 Bland–Altman: PASS Examples 1 and 2
PASS Example 1 fixes mu = 0.5, delta = 7, and conf.level = agree.level = 0.95, then crosses two power levels with three difference SDs. The comparison below keeps every row, including rows that do not agree, and reports both sample-size and achieved-power differences.

19.4.4 CMDE Appendix Case 1: Target-Value Method with Clinical Acceptance Criteria
The appendix uses the normal-approximation formula
\[
n=\frac{\left[Z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{P_0(1-P_0)}+
Z_{1-\beta}\sqrt{P_T(1-P_T)}\right]^2}{(P_T-P_0)^2}.
\]
The case uses two-sided alpha = 0.05 and power = 1 - beta = 0.80. The acceptable-standard/expected-value pairs are 85%/90% for positive agreement and 90%/94% for negative agreement. Using Z0.975 = 1.96 and Z0.80 = 0.84, the appendix reports 362 positive cases and 388 negative cases, for 750 total; after a 10% dropout allowance, at least 834 participants are enrolled.
sample_size_proportion(test = “score”, power_method = “normal”) performs the same continuous normal approximation. The package uses unrounded normal quantiles and rounds the theoretical result upward; actual alpha and power are then recalculated separately from the discrete binomial rejection region.

cmde_target_value <- data.frame(
  group = c("Positive group", "Negative group"),
  p0 = c(0.85, 0.90),
  p1 = c(0.90, 0.94),
  cmde_n = c(362L, 388L)
)

cmde_target_results <- lapply(
  seq_len(nrow(cmde_target_value)),
  function(i) {
    sample_size_proportion(
      p0 = cmde_target_value$p0[i],
      p1 = cmde_target_value$p1[i],
      alpha = 0.05,
      power = 0.80,
      alternative = "two.sided",
      test = "score",
      power_method = "normal"
    )
  }
)

title: 20  Outlier and Normality Tests
text:
20.1 Main Functions
Outlier and distribution tests help identify problems in data quality, the experimental process, or model assumptions. They are diagnostic tools before analysis, not automatic tools for deleting data or declaring a product acceptable.
This chapter introduces the independent-data functions outliers_test() and normal_test(), together with outlier() and normal() methods for mcr and precision objects. Always trace conclusions back to the original records and retain sensitivity analyses with and without candidate outliers.

title: 20  Outlier and Normality Tests
text:
Function
Main purpose




outliers_test()
Apply Grubbs, ESD, Dixon, or IQR to an ordinary data column


normal_test()
Apply Shapiro, AD, Lilliefors, or CvM to an ordinary data column


outlier()
Mark candidate outliers in an mcr or precision object


normal()
Perform normality diagnostics for a precision object


plot()
Plot diagnostic figures for test or analysis objects




20.1.1 Parameters and Formulas for Ordinary Data


Code
outliers_test(
  data, col, method = c("grubbs", "esd", "dixon", "iqr"), ...
)
normal_test(
  data, col,
  method = c("auto", "shapiro", "sw", "ad", "lillie", "cvm"),
  level = 0.95
)










Method
Core definition
Main boundary




Grubbs
\(G=\max|x_i-\bar x|/s\)
At most one point per test; alpha controls the test


Generalized ESD
Sequentially remove the largest standardized deviation and compare each \(R_i\) with its critical value
r is the maximum candidate count, default min(5,n-2)


Dixon
Endpoint spacing divided by the range, \(Q\)
Only \(3\le n\le30\); alpha only 0.01 or 0.05


IQR
Below \(Q_1-kIQR\) or above \(Q_3+kIQR\)
Descriptive rule; default coef is 1.5



Missing and nonfinite values are ignored, but indices reports one-based positions in the original vector. Grubbs, ESD, and Dixon rely on assumptions such as independence and approximate normality; IQR makes no normality assumption but is not a probability-significance test.
The deterministic mapping used by normal_test(method="auto") is:



Finite sample size
Actual method




\(n<3\)
No test


\(3\le n\le50\)
Shapiro–Wilk


\(51\le n\le5000\)
Anderson–Darling


\(n>5000\)
Lilliefors



The significance level is \(α=1-\texttt{level}\). Q-Q plots and histograms from plot() help identify skewness, heavy tails, and mixtures. P values vary strongly with sample size and must be interpreted together with the plots and data-generating process.
outliers_test() returns the method, statistic, P value, candidate outliers, and indices. normal_test() returns the actual method, statistic, P value, and sample size.
When an ordinary data frame contains multiple analytes, levels, or lots, outliers_test() and normal_test() do not group automatically. Use split_by_factors(data, variable="analyte") first, then apply the same prespecified test with lapply() to each subset. Report each group separately; do not combine all groups and test them as one sample.


20.1.2 Statistical Unit for Object-Level Methods
outlier(mcr, type="difference") tests paired differences, whereas type="candidate" or "reference" tests one method’s results; percent differences also depend on the denominator. outlier(precision) and normal(precision) process results according to groups defined by by and do not automatically reconstruct independent residuals by day or run. Object-level diagnostics are saved in object slots, so reassign the object after each call.
Object-level outlier() and normal() return updated objects with diagnostic slots; plot() returns a ggplot object.

title: 20  Outlier and Normality Tests
text:
20.2 Analysis Examples

20.2.1 Test an Ordinary Data Column


Code
library(ivdtools)


Construct teaching data containing extreme observations. In a formal project, save the raw data and data dictionary before any exclusion or transformation.


Code
diagnostic_data <- data.frame(
  sample_id = seq_len(22),
  result = c(99.8, 100.4, 99.7, 100.1, 100.0, 99.9,
             100.3, 100.2, 99.6, 100.1, 100.0, 99.8,

             100.1, 99.9, 108.0, 92.0)
)

grubbs_result <- outliers_test(diagnostic_data, "result", method = "grubbs")
iqr_result <- outliers_test(diagnostic_data, "result", method = "iqr")
normality_result <- normal_test(diagnostic_data, "result", method = "shapiro")

A P value alone cannot decide whether to delete an observation, especially for very large or very small samples; use plots, experimental records, and the study objective.


Code
plot(normality_result, type = c("qq", "his"))


















20.2.2 Outliers in a Method-Comparison Object
Make clear whether the abnormal quantity is the candidate method, the reference method, or the paired difference. First create an mcr object and then specify the detection type:


Code
mcr_data <- data.frame(
  id = 1:12,
  candidate = c(10.1, 11.2, 12.0, 13.1, 14.0, 15.2,
                16.1, 17.0, 18.2, 19.0, 20.1, 28.0),
  reference = c(10.0, 11.0, 12.1, 13.0, 14.1, 15.0,
                16.0, 17.1, 18.0, 19.1, 20.0, 21.0)
)

mcr_result <- mcr(
  mcr_data, id = "id", candidate = "candidate", reference = "reference"
)
mcr_result <- outlier(mcr_result, method = "grubbs", type = "difference")



Outlier

  Data:   Difference (candidate - reference)
  Alpha:  0.05

  1 outlier(s) found:
  Row                Value   Statistic  Critical
   -------------------------------------------------- 
  12                7.0000      3.1694  2.4116


After detecting a candidate outlier, review sample identity, run order, reagent lot, instrument alarms, and the original trace. Exclusion requires a traceable technical reason, and key results with and without the observation should both be reported.


20.2.3 Outliers and Normality in a Precision Object
Diagnostics for a precision design should preserve the experimental hierarchy; replicate results from one run must not be treated as independent patient samples.


Code
precision_data <- data.frame(
  sample = rep("level_1", 20),
  day = factor(rep(1:5, each = 4)),
  run = factor(rep(rep(1:2, each = 2), 5)),
  result = c(99.8, 100.1, 100.0, 99.9, 100.2, 100.0, 100.1, 99.8,
             99.7, 100.0, 99.9, 100.1, 100.3, 100.1, 100.0, 100.2,
             99.8, 100.0, 100.1, 100.0)
)

precision_result <- precision(precision_data, result ~ day/run, by = "sample")
precision_result <- outlier(precision_result, method = "grubbs")


Outlier detection -- Grubbs (alpha = 0.05)
  No outliers detected.


Code
precision_result <- normal(precision_result, method = "shapiro")


Normality test -- Shapiro-Wilk
  Sample               n  Method               Statistic  p-value
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  level_1             20  Shapiro-Wilk          W=0.9550  0.4497




20.2.4 Standard Case: YY/T 1789.4-2022 Appendix A.2
The standard uses 18.85, 20.38, 21.97, and 22.32 ng/mL to demonstrate Grubbs and two-sided Dixon tests, with no outlier in either test. These two entry points correspond directly to outliers_test().


Code
yyt1789_4_outlier <- data.frame(
  sample = 1:4,
  result = c(18.85, 20.38, 21.97, 22.32)
)

yyt1789_4_grubbs <- ivdtools::outliers_test(
  yyt1789_4_outlier, "result", method = "grubbs", alpha = 0.05
)
yyt1789_4_grubbs


Grubbs Outliers Test
  Data:   yyt1789_4_outlier
  Column: result (n = 4, missing = 0)
  Parameters: alpha = 0.05
  Outliers: 0

  No outliers detected.


Code
yyt1789_4_dixon <- ivdtools::outliers_test(
  yyt1789_4_outlier, "result", method = "dixon", alpha = 0.05,
  type = "both"
)
yyt1789_4_dixon


Dixon Q Outliers Test
  Data:   yyt1789_4_outlier
  Column: result (n = 4, missing = 0)
  Parameters: alpha = 0.05, type = both
  Outliers: 0

  No outliers detected.


Both package functions report zero outliers, consistent with the standard. The standard displays Grubbs statistics of 1.2727 at the low end and 0.9028 at the high end, and Dixon statistics of 0.441 at the low end and 0.101 at the high end. The current print method reports only outlier positions and conclusions, not these intermediate statistics; “conclusions agree” must not be written as “all intermediate values were reproduced.”

title: 21  Introduction to Algorithm Principles
text:
21.1 Replicates, Multiple Samples, and Statistical Units
This chapter explains how to choose statistical units, connect the main ivdtools workflows, and understand what key arguments change mathematically. It is intended as a bridge between function documentation and audit of the implementation.

title: 21  Introduction to Algorithm Principles
text:
21.1.1 First Decide What One Row Represents
Before choosing a function, identify whether one row is a patient/sample result, a replicate measurement, a run, a bottle, a time point, or a paired method result. Replicates are not automatically independent subjects. If a function expects sample-level means, aggregate according to the protocol and preserve replicate count and SD.
Functions that can receive replicate results directly include precision(), linearity(), interference_*(), dilution_recovery(), spike_recovery(), sensitivity_*(), and c5_c95() when their grouping arguments are supplied. Functions that require paired or sample-level results include mcr(), roc(), raw_to_table(), reference_interval(), and many sample-size calculations. Check the help page and define the analysis unit before reshaping data.


21.1.2 Joint or Separate Analysis for Multiple Samples
Use by when the function is designed to estimate every sample or concentration separately, such as precision(..., by="sample"). Use a common model only when the scientific question and variance structure require pooling. split_by_factors() and split_by_cutpoints() create named data lists for independent, prespecified analyses; they must not be used repeatedly to search for a favorable result.

title: 21  Introduction to Algorithm Principles
text:
21.2 Outliers and Normality

21.2.1 Grubbs Test
For a finite sample, the Grubbs statistic is
\[G=\frac{\max_i|x_i-\bar x|}{s}.\]
The test generally identifies at most one point per call and assumes independent, approximately normal observations. A flagged observation is a candidate for investigation, not an instruction to delete it.


21.2.2 Generalized ESD
Generalized ESD removes the most extreme standardized observation sequentially and compares each \(R_i\) with a critical value. r is the maximum number of candidate points; it does not mean that r points will be removed.


21.2.3 Dixon and IQR
Dixon uses an endpoint spacing divided by the range and is limited to small samples, currently \(3\le n\le30\) with alpha 0.01 or 0.05. IQR flags values below \(Q_1-kIQR\) or above \(Q_3+kIQR\) and is descriptive rather than a probability test.


21.2.4 Automatic Normality Branch
normal_test(method="auto") uses a deterministic sample-size rule:



Sample size
Test




\(n<3\)
No test


\(3\le n\le50\)
Shapiro–Wilk


\(51\le n\le5000\)
Anderson–Darling


\(n>5000\)
Lilliefors



P values depend strongly on sample size. Interpret them with Q-Q plots, histograms, experimental records, and the assumptions of the downstream model.

title: 21  Introduction to Algorithm Principles
text:
21.3 Method Comparison and Reference-Material Bias

21.3.1 Direction, Units, and Preprocessing
In mcr(), the candidate is Y and the reference is X; candidate-minus-reference differences and percent denominators must be recorded. A log transformation, unit conversion, or prespecified cutpoint changes the estimand and should be treated as a separate analysis.


21.3.2 Correlation Options
Pearson measures linear co-variation, Spearman measures monotone rank association, and Kendall measures concordance of ranks. None is an agreement measure. Use regression and Bland–Altman methods for bias and agreement.


21.3.3 Regression Methods










Method
X error
Y variance
Point-estimate principle
Typical use




ols
Negligible
Constant or optional weights
Minimize vertical squared residuals
Reference X has negligible error


wls
Negligible
Changes with concentration
Weighted vertical residuals
Difference SD/CV changes with concentration


deming
Included
Constant error ratio \(λ\)
Errors-in-variables regression
Both procedures have measurement error


wdeming
Included
Common weights, constant CV, or precision profiles
Weighted/iterative errors-in-variables fit
Error changes with concentration


pb
Included
No normal-error assumption
Rank estimate of pairwise slopes
Linear relation with outliers or mixed variation



OLS minimizes \(\sum_i(y_i-a-bx_i)^2\). Weighted regression minimizes a weighted version. Deming uses the relative error variance \(λ\) and should estimate it from independent precision evidence. Passing–Bablok is robust to some outliers but is not a guarantee against every data problem.
Common WLS weights include 1/y, 1/y^2, 1/x, 1/x^2, constant_cv, residual, and a user-supplied nonnegative finite column. 1/x^2 represents constant CV on the reference scale; residual updates a concentration-dependent residual SD and is iterative.


21.3.4 Confidence Intervals and Bland–Altman
ci_method="auto" uses analytic covariance for OLS/WLS, jackknife refitting for Deming variants, and rank intervals for Passing–Bablok. Bootstrap methods require enough replicates and a fixed seed for reproducibility. Bland–Altman center, SD, and LoA describe the distribution of paired differences; agree.level controls the proportion covered by LoA, whereas conf.level controls uncertainty in the estimated LoA.


21.3.5 Reference-Material Bias
Reference-material bias is not the same as clinical-sample method-comparison bias. reference_bias() combines the measurement-mean uncertainty and assigned-value uncertainty when supplied. State the assigned-value source, its uncertainty, the bias direction, and whether the material is commutable.

title: 21  Introduction to Algorithm Principles
text:
21.4 Reference-Material Commutability
EP14/EP30 methods compare materials with the clinical-sample procedure relationship, usually using Deming prediction intervals. IFCC Part 2 compares reference-material bias with clinical-sample bias and combines uncertainty. IFCC Part 3 evaluates before/after calibration. Different paths can produce different conclusions because they target different estimands.

title: 21  Introduction to Algorithm Principles
text:
21.5 Qualitative Performance, C5/C95, and ROC
For a four-fold table \(a=TP,b=FP,c=FN,d=TN\),
\[Se=\frac{a}{a+c},\quad Sp=\frac{d}{b+d},\quad
PPV=\frac{a}{a+b},\quad NPV=\frac{d}{c+d}.\]
Kappa adjusts observed agreement for marginal agreement; PABAK uses \(2P_o-1\) and is not the same estimand. McNemar uses discordant pairs. C5/C95 solve for mean responses whose modeled positive probability is 0.05 or 0.95, using a precision profile. ROC AUC is the probability of correctly ranking a random positive above a random negative under the selected direction; it is not accuracy at a cutoff.

title: 21  Introduction to Algorithm Principles
section: 21.6 Precision, Bottle Variation, and Reference Intervals
text:
21.6 Precision, Bottle Variation, and Reference Intervals
For nested precision designs, total variance is the sum of variance components. variance() estimates components, ci() estimates intervals, and profile() models concentration-related SD/CV. Bottle ANOVA tests group means; it does not quantify whether a difference is practically acceptable. uncertainty_homogeneity() produces a standard uncertainty component.
Reference intervals have two independent settings: central coverage interval and endpoint confidence ci. Nonparametric, biweight, type-6, parametric, and Huber methods make different distributional and robust-estimation assumptions. A normality or outlier test is not an automatic method-selection or deletion rule.

title: 21  Introduction to Algorithm Principles
text:
21.7 Response-Equation Fitting and Linearity
fit_equation() fits registered response equations such as linear, quadratic, exponential, power, 4PLC, 5PLC, Gaussian, Michaelis–Menten, sinusoidal, and cubic forms. Equation fitting describes calibration response and should not be confused with EP06 method linearity. linearity() specifically evaluates level means, residuals, weights, and ADL. A high calibration \(R^2\) does not establish method linearity.

title: 21  Introduction to Algorithm Principles
section: 21.8 Interference, Dilution, Spike Recovery, and Hook Effect
text:
21.8 Interference, Dilution, Spike Recovery, and Hook Effect
Paired interference estimates a test-minus-control effect; dose response estimates how that effect changes with interferent concentration; patient-sample comparison assesses method differences in the presence of a factor. Dilution recovery corrects results by the dilution factor, spike recovery compares an observed increment with a theoretical mass-balance increment, and hook-effect analysis uses raw response at known high concentrations.

title: 21  Introduction to Algorithm Principles
text:
21.9 Analytical Sensitivity
LoB describes the blank upper tail, LoD describes distinguishability from blank, and LoQ adds a precision or total-error criterion. sensitivity_lob(), sensitivity_lod(), sensitivity_loq(), and sensitivity_verify() keep establishment and verification separate. A reported LoQ is constrained not to be below LoD when LoD is supplied.

title: 21  Introduction to Algorithm Principles
text:
21.10 Quality Control and Stability
For QC, \(z_i=(x_i-\mu_0)/\sigma_0\). The current rules use strict \(>2\), \(>3\), and \(>1\) thresholds for 1-2s, 1-3s, and 4-1s, while R-4s uses \(|z|\ge2\) and a range \(|\Delta z|\ge4\). qc_chart() scans one sequence in row order; it does not implement cross-level multirule decisions. Stability functions estimate node bias, time trends, time to a limit, Arrhenius acceleration, and MKT; they do not turn a model extrapolation into observed evidence.

title: 21  Introduction to Algorithm Principles
text:
21.11 Measurement Uncertainty and Traceability
Type A components come from statistical repeatability or replication; Type B components come from certificates, limits, distributions, or prior information. uncertainty_combine() combines standard uncertainties, uncertainty_propagate() applies a measurement model, and uncertainty_traceability() accumulates components across a traceability chain. Record the input quantity, standard uncertainty, sensitivity coefficient, degrees of freedom, covariance assumptions, and coverage factor.

title: 21  Introduction to Algorithm Principles
text:
21.13 Detailed Algorithm Specification

21.13.1 OLS and WLS Point Estimates
Ordinary least squares minimizes
\[
Q(a,b)=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-a-bx_i)^2.
\]
Weighted least squares minimizes
\[
Q_w(a,b)=\sum_{i=1}^n w_i(y_i-a-bx_i)^2.
\]
Let
\[
W=\sum_iw_i,\qquad
\bar x_w=\frac{\sum_iw_ix_i}{W},\qquad
\bar y_w=\frac{\sum_iw_iy_i}{W},
\]
\[
S_{xx,w}=\sum_iw_i(x_i-\bar x_w)^2,\qquad
S_{xy,w}=\sum_iw_i(x_i-\bar x_w)(y_i-\bar y_w).
\]
Then
\[
\hat b=\frac{S_{xy,w}}{S_{xx,w}},\qquad
\hat a=\bar y_w-\hat b\bar x_w.
\]
OLS is the special case w_i = 1. The weight choices change the assumed concentration dependence of the error variance:
